introduction: This guide is about the life of feeling that the writings call spiritual: the heart's capacity to be moved by love, gladness, longing and sorrow that do not come from the senses. The readings kept here distinguish two kinds of susceptibility in a person, describe the inner eye and ear, speak of joy in good news and patience in separation, of hearts that reflect one another like mirrors, and end in prayers of thirst. The quotations set beside them come from people who knew these states and wrote them down: the Psalms and the Song of Songs, Paul, Augustine, Pascal, Rumi, the Qur’an, Wordsworth, Donne and Herbert. Others test the readings: Hume gives feeling the rule over reason, the Dhammapada and the Stoics advise loving less or minding less, and Adam Smith and Matthew Arnold report how little the heart sometimes feels.
questions: The readings speak of two kinds of susceptibility in every person. How, in practice, do you tell a feeling that clouds the mirror from one that polishes it?
Pascal says the heart has reasons that reason does not know; Hume says reason only serves the passions. What part does thinking play in the feelings these readings describe?
Several readings say that longing grows stronger in separation. When has distance from something you love made you understand it better?
The readings picture hearts as mirrors that reflect one another, and Adam Smith notes how little we feel for those far away. What widens the reach of a person’s sympathy?
The Dhammapada and the Stoics advise guarding against strong attachment, while these readings praise thirst. What is each afraid of, and what is each right about?
Which reading or quotation here describes a state you recognise, and what brought it about?

outside.why: Augustine opens his Confessions with the same thought: the heart is made for somewhere else and is restless until it rests there.
Paul's hymn to love describes it by what it does and refuses to do, and says it is the one thing that never fails.
Dante ends his poem with a love that moves the sun and the other stars: attraction as the law of the whole creation.
Darwin grants humanity a sympathy that reaches the humblest creature, and says we still bear the stamp of a lowly origin. Does a feeling's history tell us what it is worth?
Pascal's famous sentence makes the same distinction between two ways of knowing: the heart has reasons that reason does not know.
This is the account in Acts that the reading retells: the disciples together in one place, and the sound and the fire that came upon them.
The bystanders at Pentecost said the disciples were full of new wine; the picture of wine for spiritual gladness is an old one.
The Qur’an says a reminder reaches the one who has a heart, or who gives ear with full attention.
The beatitude ties sight to the state of the heart: it is the pure in heart who shall see God.
The Qur’an says the same of the heedless: it is not the eyes that grow blind but the hearts within the breasts.
Paul lists what life in the spirit yields, and the list is made of states of the heart: love, joy, peace, gentleness.
Wordsworth describes a quiet in which the powers work together, and says that in it we see into the life of things.
The Qur’an uses the same comparison for those who have hearts and do not understand with them: they are like cattle, or further astray.
The poet, looking at a beautiful valley, felt a presence in it that was more than the scenery before his eyes.
Pascal warns that a human being is neither angel nor brute, and that whoever tries to play the angel ends by playing the brute. Is there a danger in thinking of ourselves as wholly spiritual?
Wordsworth's complaint is the reading's own: in getting and spending we lay waste our powers and give our hearts away.
Paul speaks of things that eye has not seen nor ear heard, which are made known in another way, by the Spirit.
Hume holds that reason is and ought to be the slave of the passions. If feeling rules in any case, what makes one feeling dust on the mirror and another its polish?
Plato pictures the soul as a driver with two horses, one noble and one unruly, which is very near the reading's two kinds of susceptibility.
The psalm invites its hearers to taste and see that the Lord is good, as though there were a palate for such things.
The Qur’an describes true believers as those whose hearts feel fear when God is mentioned, and whose faith grows when His verses are recited.
The Dhammapada compares fine words that are not acted on to a beautiful flower that has no scent.
The Dhammapada draws the opposite conclusion from the changeableness of affection: love nothing, since losing what is loved is pain. Is the answer to fickle love less love, or a truer one?
Pascal traced the restlessness of the world to one cause: people cannot stay quietly in their own room.
Pascal holds the same two thoughts together: a human being is a reed, the weakest thing in nature, and yet greater than the universe that crushes it.
Paul speaks of a law written in the heart, with conscience bearing witness to it in those who never heard the commandments.
The proverb observed long ago that the state of the heart acts on the body: a merry heart does good like a medicine.
The Qur’an says in a single line what the reading says with rain and flowers: in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest.
Augustine was moved to tears by the singing in church and then worried that the melody moved him more than the words. How can a person tell tenderness in worship from pleasure in it?
The Song of Songs also speaks of a love better than wine; the language of this prayer has a long ancestry.
The psalmist's thirst is of the kind the reading praises: as the deer pants for the brooks, so the soul pants after God.
Matthew Arnold stood on a beach and heard the sea of faith only as a long withdrawing roar. What makes the same sea a wave lapping at the heart for one person and an ebb for another?
Shelley prays to the wind to make him its lyre: the wish to be an instrument that a greater breath plays through.
Isaiah's promise is in the same future tense: the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose.
The psalmist longs to see the power and glory as he once saw them in the sanctuary, and his whole body shares the longing.
The elder who writes the third letter of John says the same: he has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in truth.
Mary's song in Luke is the rejoicing of a woman of low estate who has been regarded and lifted up.
Paul too falls silent about what he was shown: words were heard that it is not possible to utter.
The Song of Songs gives lovers their shortest creed: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
In the Song of Songs the winter is past, flowers appear, and the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in the land.
Mencius marvels that people search for a lost fowl or dog and do not think to search for their own lost heart.
The lover in the Song of Songs rises at night and goes about the city seeking the one her soul loves.
The two disciples at Emmaus say afterwards that their hearts burned within them while he talked with them on the road.
Rumi's reed-flute sings of its longing for the reed-bed it was cut from, and all who hear it are stirred.
The psalm greets a day in the same spirit: this is the day the Lord has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
The Dhammapada says that the scent of flowers cannot travel against the wind, but the fragrance of good people goes everywhere.
The psalm is a summons to shared gladness: come, let us sing, let us make a joyful noise.
The Preacher thinks the house of mourning a better place than the house of feasting, since sorrow improves the heart. Is all sorrow born of matter, or does some of it teach?
Epictetus taught that people are disturbed by their judgments about things and not by the things. How far is the reading's certitude the same remedy, and where does it differ?
Keats says that a thing of beauty is a joy for ever, and that its loveliness increases.
The psalm promises nearness to exactly such a person: the Lord is close to those of a broken heart.
Paul writes to friends that he has been taken from them in presence and not in heart, and longs to see their faces.
Donne tells the one he must leave that their parting is not a breach but an expansion, like gold beaten out thin.
George Herbert is surprised to find his shrivelled heart green again after a hard season.
The psalmist speaks to his own soul as the reading speaks to its reader: why are you cast down? Hope in God.
In the Book of Revelation the voice is at the door, knocking, and waits for anyone who hears it and opens.
Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted. Does honouring a mother's sacrifice leave room for a grief like hers?
Pascal says it is the heart that experiences God and not the reason, and that this is what faith is.
Marcus Aurelius asks to be like the headland on which the waves keep breaking while it stands and the water grows calm around it.
Shelley ends his ode with the same question the reading answers: if winter comes, can spring be far behind?
This is the saying of Jesus that the reading begins from: the light of the body is the eye.
Aristotle thought that no one would choose to live without friends, even if he had every other good.
Shakespeare's Lorenzo distrusts the person who has no music in himself and is not moved by sweet sounds.
The Book of Samuel says that the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and he loved him as his own soul.
The proverb has the same picture of a reflecting surface: as face answers to face in water, so one heart answers another.
Adam Smith observes that a man would lose more sleep over his own little finger than over the ruin of a distant multitude. If hearts are mirrors, why do they reflect so little from far away?
The Qur’an says that no amount of spending could have attuned those hearts to each other; it was God who attuned them.
Tennyson's dying king asks to be prayed for, and says more things are wrought by prayer than the world dreams of.
The Buddha told his community that it would prosper so long as its members met often and met in concord.
The sonnet turns at the same point: if I think on thee, dear friend, all losses are restored.
Paul also knows a speech beyond words: the Spirit pleads for us with groanings that cannot be uttered.
The psalm speaks of a language without speech or words whose sound nonetheless goes out through all the earth.
Jeremiah foresees a covenant written in the heart, so that no one need say to a neighbour, Know the Lord.
Emily Dickinson never saw a moor or the sea and was sure she knew them. What does a picture of a face add for someone who already loves?
Emerson defines a friend as a person with whom he may be sincere and before whom he may think aloud.
Seneca advises staying away from crowds, since we always bring back some fault we caught there. If feeling passes from one person to another, how do we choose what we catch?
The Song of Songs claims the same lastingness for love: it is strong as death, and many waters cannot quench it.
Paul asks the Philippians to complete his joy by being of one accord and of one mind.
Paul's rule for a community is the feeling in this reading: rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep.
James draws the same line between two kinds of listening: be doers of the word, and not hearers only.
The Dhammapada gives the same order: let each first direct himself to what is right, and then teach others.
The Qur’an tells the Prophet that it was by gentleness that he kept people near him; had he been harsh they would have scattered.
John Wesley wrote down the evening hour at which, listening to a reading, he felt his heart strangely warmed.
The Qur’an asks the Prophet to keep company with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face.
The Qur’an promises the righteous a pure wine, sealed; the cup in this reading belongs to the same family of pictures.
Krishna asks that whatever a person does or gives be made an offering, which is what the sheared tresses were.
Paul says that the things of the Spirit look like foolishness to one who has no sense for them.
The invitation has the tone of one in the Gospel: come unto me, all that labour, and I will give you rest.
Augustine prays out of the same sense of his own helplessness: give what You command, and command what You will.
Spinoza holds that one who loves God cannot strive that God should love him in return. Is the thirst in this prayer a wish to be loved back, or something else?
Thomas à Kempis begins his book by calling everything vanity except to love God and to serve Him only.
The Imitation of Christ praises love as the thing that makes every heavy burden light and every bitter thing sweet.
Jesus tells the woman at the well of a water after which no one thirsts again, springing up within the one who drinks.
Augustine addresses God as a beauty ancient and new that he loved too late, having looked for it outside himself.
The first letter of Peter tells its readers not to think a fiery trial strange, and to rejoice in sharing such sufferings.
Epictetus advises wishing that things happen as they do happen. Is the acceptance in this prayer the Stoic's calm, or does love change what is being accepted?
The psalmist, hunted every day, asks that his tears be kept in God's bottle and written in His book.
Emily Dickinson describes what follows great pain as a formal feeling, stiff and cold as lead. Do the tears and burning in this reading belong to a different kind of suffering?
Tagore pictures himself as a small reed flute through which melodies eternally new are breathed.
Donne begs God to do more than knock at his heart: to break it and make it new.
